items.zh: 四無量心 · 修悲證悲

zh: 第二、釋修證悲，即為二：一者、正明修悲方法，如佛說：「若有比丘以悲相應心，無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，善修。」悲相應心者，行者於慈定中常念欲與眾生樂，從慈定起，猶見眾生受種種身苦、心苦，心生憐愍，即作是念：「眾生可念，莫令受是種種身苦、心苦。」復更念言：「我今無目，五道之中親、中、怨人並受種種身心諸苦，而我不知不見，長夜懈怠，不生救拔之心。」作是念已，即發願言：「若有眾生受種種苦，我於定中悉願得見，勤加救護。」
en: Second, explaining the cultivation and realization of compassion: this itself has two parts.

First, directly clarifying the method of cultivating compassion, as the Buddha says: "There is a monk who, with a mind corresponding to compassion, free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable, cultivates it well." As for the mind corresponding with compassion: the practitioner, within the concentration of loving-kindness, constantly holds the wish to give sentient beings happiness; arising from this concentration of loving-kindness, one nonetheless still sees sentient beings undergoing various kinds of bodily and mental suffering, and a mind of pity arises, reflecting: "Sentient beings are pitiable — may they not have to undergo these various kinds of bodily and mental suffering." One reflects further still: "I have, until now, been without eyes — throughout the five realms, loved ones, neutral persons, and enemies alike all undergo these various kinds of bodily and mental suffering, and yet I, neither knowing nor seeing it, have spent the long night in idleness, never giving rise to a mind that would rescue them." Having reflected in this way, one then makes this vow: "Should there be sentient beings undergoing various kinds of suffering, may I, within concentration, come to see this in every case, and diligently apply myself to rescuing and protecting them."

zh: 作是願已，即入禪定，用定念淨心先取一所愛親人受苦之相，繫心緣之。若有異念，攝之令還，令於心想的的分明，其心憐愍，悲念無極，如是乃至中、怨、憎一方，乃至十方，一道乃至五道亦如是，是則略說修悲方法。二、明悲定發相。行者福德智慧善根清淨，作是觀時，三昧便發，即於定中見於親人受苦之相，了了分明，其心悲愍，欲加救護。既見親人受苦，生憐愍心已，次見中人、怨人如是，乃至十方、五道眾生受苦之相。行者於定心中見外人受苦，而內心憐愍，從悲定起，心轉深固，定心與外相應，湛然無動，是名悲相應心。無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，皆如上說。
en: Having made this vow, one then enters dhyāna-concentration, using the pure mind of concentration and mindfulness to first take up the mark of a single loved one's own suffering, fixing the mind upon it as its object. Should some other thought arise, one gathers the mind back in, making the mental image entirely clear and distinct, the mind full of pity, compassionate regard without limit — extending, in this way, to a neutral person, an enemy, one to be hated, then to a single direction, and, further still, to all ten directions; to a single realm, and, further still, to all five realms, following the same pattern. This, in brief, describes the method for cultivating compassion.

Second, clarifying the mark of the compassion concentration's own arising. The practitioner, through the purity of merit, wisdom, and wholesome roots, contemplating in this way, samādhi is thereupon brought forth; one sees, within concentration, the mark of the loved one's own suffering, entirely clear and distinct, the mind full of compassionate pity, wishing to rescue and protect them. Having seen the loved one undergoing suffering, and a mind of pity having arisen, one next sees the same for a neutral person and an enemy, and, further still, for sentient beings throughout the ten directions and all five realms undergoing suffering. The practitioner, seeing others undergoing suffering within the concentrated mind, while the inward mind of pity, arising from the concentration of compassion, grows ever deeper and more secure, the concentrated mind corresponding with what is seen without, deep and unmoving — this is named the mind corresponding with compassion. Free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable — all exactly as already described above.

zh: 善修者，於悲定中非但見親人受苦，深憐愍，乃至中、怨九種、十方、五道諸受苦者，憐愍救護，其心平等，故名善修。復次，若見是受苦之人生愍念，受樂者、受不苦不樂者而不憐念，不名善修；若見三種之人悉皆是苦，憐愍不二，是名善修。復次，見五道眾生受苦差別，名不善修；若見受苦不異，憐愍平等，名曰善修。亦可得言：若見五道眾生受苦一種，名不善修；若能分別五道眾生受苦差別不同，名曰善修。如是略說善修之相。
en: As for "cultivated well": within the concentration of compassion, not merely seeing a loved one undergo suffering and feeling deep pity for them, but extending this, all the way through the nine kinds of person, neutral and enemy alike, and to every being undergoing suffering throughout the ten directions and the five realms, feeling pity and offering rescue and protection with a mind held perfectly equal throughout — this is what is named cultivating it well. Furthermore: if, seeing one undergoing suffering, pity arises, but toward one experiencing happiness, or one experiencing neither suffering nor happiness, no such pitying regard arises at all, this cannot be named cultivating it well; only if, seeing all three kinds of person, one recognizes that each, in their own way, is equally undergoing suffering, and holds pity for them without any distinction, is this named cultivating it well. Furthermore: seeing sentient beings across the five realms as undergoing differing kinds of suffering is not named cultivating it well; seeing that the suffering they undergo is, at root, not different at all, and holding pity for them equally, is what is named cultivating it well. It may also, however, be said the other way: seeing sentient beings across the five realms as undergoing a single, uniform kind of suffering is not named cultivating it well; being able to properly distinguish the differing kinds of suffering sentient beings across the five realms actually undergo is what is named cultivating it well. This, in brief, describes the mark of cultivating it well.

zh: 問曰：五道眾生果報不同，苦樂有異，如三塗眾生多苦報，人道眾生半受苦樂，天道眾生多受樂果。云何行慈因緣皆見一切受樂，行悲因緣皆見一切受苦，豈非顛倒耶？答曰：不然，是為得解之道。行者欲學是慈無量心時，先當作願：「願諸眾生受種種樂。」取受樂人相，攝心入定，即見眾生皆悉受樂。譬如鑽火，先以軟草、乾牛糞等，火勢轉大，能燒大濕。大慈心初發亦如是。初生之火，唯及親人，慈心轉廣，怨親同等，皆見受樂，無復苦相。復次，一切眾生五道輪轉，苦樂不定，即雖暫樂，後必大苦，今雖大苦，後當得樂。雖即未然，必有其事。是故行者用得解之心，緣於一切皆樂，不墮顛倒。悲、喜、捨心亦復如是。
en: Question: sentient beings across the five realms have differing karmic results, their suffering and happiness differing accordingly — beings in the three lower realms undergo, for the most part, suffering as their karmic result; beings in the human realm receive suffering and happiness in roughly equal measure; and beings in the heavenly realms receive, for the most part, happiness as their karmic result. How, then, can the causes and conditions of practicing loving-kindness lead one to see all beings alike receiving happiness, while the causes and conditions of practicing compassion lead one to see all beings alike undergoing suffering — is this not itself a form of inverted, deluded thinking? Answer: this does not follow; this is, rather, the path of understanding attained — an understanding deliberately brought to mind in contemplation.

The practitioner, wishing to study this immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, should first make this vow: "May all sentient beings receive every kind of happiness." Taking up the mark of a person receiving happiness, gathering the mind and entering concentration, one thereby comes to see sentient beings all receiving happiness. It is like starting a fire by friction: using soft grass and dried cattle-dung at first, the fire's own strength gradually grows greater, until it is able to burn even what is thoroughly damp. The great mind of loving-kindness, at its first arising, is exactly the same: the fire, at its very first kindling, reaches only a loved one, but, as the mind of loving-kindness grows ever wider, enemy and loved one alike are seen equally, all receiving happiness, with no mark of suffering left at all.

Furthermore: every sentient being, turning through the five realms, has suffering and happiness that are themselves never fixed — though there be happiness for the moment, great suffering is bound to follow later; and though there be great suffering now, happiness is bound to be attained later as well. Though this has not yet actually come to pass, it is nonetheless bound to occur. Hence the practitioner, using this mind of understanding attained, takes every being as receiving happiness alike, without falling into any inverted, deluded thinking at all. The minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are exactly the same in this respect.

The nine-fold grid of persons (three grades each of loved one, neutral person, and enemy) recurs from loving-kindness into compassion unchanged — the same diagnostic structure, different content held in mind. The two competing definitions of "cultivated well" offered back-to-back at the end (seeing suffering as fundamentally undifferentiated versus being able to distinguish its different kinds precisely) are presented as equally valid without forcing a choice between them, consistent with how this treatise generally treats apparently competing formulations as complementary rather than as rivals to be resolved. The fire-by-friction and impermanence arguments answering the "isn't this delusion" objection apply symmetrically to compassion's own seeming inversion (seeing beings in bliss as also, truly, in need of rescue) — the same logic run in the opposite direction.

items.zh: 四無量心 · 修喜證喜

zh: 第三、釋修喜證喜，即為二：一者、正明修喜方法，如佛說：「若比丘以喜相應心，無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，善修。」喜相應心者，行者入悲定已，其心愍傷一切眾生長夜為諸苦惱之所逼迫，我當云何而拔濟之，令是等眾生從苦得樂，從樂生歡喜？爾時深觀眾生雖受苦惱，此苦虛妄，本無今有，易可除滅。所以者何？如人有病苦，若遇良藥，即便差愈，更以衣食供給，快樂無量。復次，如人火熱，身受苦惱，若得清冷之水，火苦即滅，歡樂便生。如人現受貧困，以是因緣，慳貪造惡，若給施珍寶，教修布施行善，則現在離於貧弊，身心慶快，未來之世長受安樂。復次，又如世人愚癡顛倒，縈纏煩惱，受種種苦，若聞無漏清淨妙法，如說修行，煩惱病除，即便獲得禪定、智慧及涅槃樂。如是種種因緣，苦無定性，易可除滅，令得歡樂。
en: Third, explaining the cultivation and realization of sympathetic joy: this itself has two parts.

First, directly clarifying the method of cultivating sympathetic joy, as the Buddha says: "There is a monk who, with a mind corresponding to sympathetic joy, free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable, cultivates it well." As for the mind corresponding with sympathetic joy: the practitioner, having entered the concentration of compassion, the mind grieves over how every sentient being has, throughout the long night, been oppressed by every kind of suffering and affliction — how, then, should I go about rescuing and delivering them, so that these very sentient beings may pass from suffering into happiness, and, from happiness, give rise to delight? At this point, one deeply contemplates that, although sentient beings undergo suffering and affliction, this suffering is itself illusory, originally absent and only now present, and so easily removed and extinguished.

Why is this? It is like a person suffering from illness: should they encounter the right medicine, they are cured at once, and, further supplied with clothing and food, immeasurable happiness follows. Furthermore: it is like a person burning with fever, the body suffering greatly — should they obtain cool, refreshing water, the suffering of the fever is extinguished at once, and joy and happiness arise instead. It is like a person presently suffering poverty and hardship, and, through this very cause and condition, committing wrongdoing out of stinginess and greed — should they be given precious treasure, and taught to practice generosity and cultivate goodness, they would, in the present, be freed from poverty's own hardship, body and mind rejoicing, and, in the world to come, long enjoy peace and happiness. Furthermore: it is like people in the world, deluded and inverted, bound up in affliction, undergoing every kind of suffering — should they hear the uncontaminated, pure, wondrous Dharma, and practice accordingly as it is taught, the illness of affliction is removed, and dhyāna-concentration, wisdom, and the happiness of nirvāṇa are thereby obtained at once. Through such various causes and conditions as these, suffering has no fixed nature of its own, and so is easily removed and extinguished, allowing happiness and delight to be attained.

zh: 行者作是觀已，即發願言：「願諸眾生一切諸苦悉皆除滅，受樂歡喜，我於定中悉皆得見。」作是願已，即入禪定，用念清淨心取於親人，從苦得脫，受樂歡喜相，一心觀之，令於念心的的分明，見於親人受歡樂相，其心悅豫，欣慶無量。次緣中人、怨人，乃至十方、五道眾生受喜之相，心生慶悅。是則略明修喜方法。二者、明喜定發相。行者如是修已，念慧福德善根力故，作是緣時，即發三昧力故，即於定中任運見於所愛親人離苦得樂歡喜之相，了了分明，於三昧中，其心悅豫不可說，乃至十方、五道眾生受於歡喜亦復如是。行者於三昧中見於外人受喜之相，而於內心無有動轉，定漸增深，是名喜相應心。無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，善修之義，如慈心中說。
en: The practitioner, having made this contemplation, then makes this vow: "May every suffering of every sentient being be entirely removed and extinguished, that they may receive happiness and delight — may I come to see this, in every case, within concentration." Having made this vow, one then enters dhyāna-concentration, using a mind of pure mindfulness to take up a loved one, freed from suffering and receiving the mark of happiness and delight, contemplating this single-mindedly, making the mental image entirely clear and distinct, seeing the mark of the loved one receiving joy and happiness, the mind delighted, rejoicing beyond measure. One then extends this to a neutral person, an enemy, and, further still, to sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the five realms receiving this same joy, the mind giving rise to delight. This, in brief, describes the method for cultivating sympathetic joy.

Second, clarifying the mark of the sympathetic-joy concentration's own arising. The practitioner, having cultivated in this way, through the power of mindfulness, wisdom, merit, and wholesome roots, taking up this object, samādhi is thereupon brought forth through its own power; one sees, within concentration, spontaneously and without effort, the mark of the loved one, freed from suffering, receiving happiness and delight, entirely clear and distinct — within this samādhi, the mind's own delight beyond all description; and, further still, sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the five realms receiving this same delight, exactly the same. The practitioner, seeing others receiving delight within samādhi, while the inward mind remains unmoved, concentration gradually growing ever deeper — this is named the mind corresponding with sympathetic joy. Free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable, and the sense of "cultivated well" — all exactly as already described within loving-kindness.

zh: 問曰：慈心令眾生樂，喜心令眾生喜。樂之與喜，有何等異？答曰：如《摩訶衍》中說，身樂名樂，心樂名喜。五識相應名樂，意識相應名喜。五塵中生樂名樂，法塵中生樂名喜。復次，欲界中五識相應名樂，初禪中三識相應名樂，三禪中一切樂是名樂，欲界及初禪意識相應名樂。二禪中一切樂是名喜，麁樂名樂，細樂名喜。因時名樂，果時名喜。初得樂時名樂，歡心內發，樂相外現，歡喜踊躍是名喜。樂根相應名為樂，喜根相應故名喜。如是等種種分別喜、樂之相異。
en: Question: loving-kindness gives sentient beings happiness, and sympathetic joy gives sentient beings delight — what, then, is the actual difference between happiness and delight? Answer: as the Mahāyāna treatise says, bodily happiness is named "happiness," and mental happiness is named "delight." Corresponding with the five sense-consciousnesses is named "happiness"; corresponding with mind-consciousness is named "delight." Happiness arising from the five sense-objects is named "happiness"; happiness arising from the dharma-object is named "delight." Furthermore: within the desire realm, correspondence with the five consciousnesses is named "happiness"; within the first dhyāna, correspondence with the three consciousnesses is named "happiness"; within the third dhyāna, every kind of happiness whatsoever is named "happiness"; and, within both the desire realm and the first dhyāna, correspondence with mind-consciousness specifically is named "happiness" as well. Within the second dhyāna, every kind of happiness whatsoever is named "delight." Coarse happiness is named "happiness"; fine happiness is named "delight." At the time of its cause, it is named "happiness"; at the time of its result, it is named "delight." At the very moment happiness is first attained, this is named "happiness"; a delighted mind arising within, its mark of happiness manifesting without, delight leaping up — this is named "delight." Correspondence with the happiness-faculty is named "happiness"; correspondence with the joy-faculty is named "delight." Such various distinctions as these mark the difference between the marks of delight and happiness.

zh: 問曰：若爾者，何以不慈、喜次第？答曰：行慈心時，愛念眾生猶如赤子，心願與樂，出慈三昧，猶見眾生受種種苦，深心愛念，欲拔其苦，令得安樂。當如初樂後喜，中隔於悲，故不次慈記喜也。譬如人母，雖常念子，令得安樂，而未名喜，後見染病，其心愁毒。病既得差，家業付之，大歡喜故，次悲說喜也。問曰：何故約禪明喜、樂，喜即為麁，約無量心明喜則為細？答曰：禪則以定為貴，樂心恬靜，與定相扶，故為勝。無量則心緣眾生，因緣眾生歡喜為勝，故細。復次，行者初定既淺，但以樂緣眾生。何以故？若取喜相，心散難攝，後緣三昧漸深，雖歡喜踊躍，心不散亂，故為細。
en: Question: if this is so, why are loving-kindness and sympathetic joy not spoken of in direct sequence with one another? Answer: when practicing loving-kindness, one holds sentient beings in loving regard exactly as one would one's own newborn child, the mind wishing to give them happiness; and, emerging from the concentration of loving-kindness, one nonetheless still sees sentient beings undergoing every kind of suffering, a deep and loving regard wishing to draw out this suffering and bring them to peace and happiness instead. This should follow the pattern of happiness first, delight afterward, with compassion set between them — hence sympathetic joy is not spoken of in direct sequence right after loving-kindness. It is like a mother: though she constantly holds her child in mind, wishing them peace and happiness, this alone is not yet named delight; but later, seeing the child fall ill, her own mind is consumed with anguish and grief — and, once the illness is cured, and the family's own fortune is entrusted to the child, great delight follows. Hence sympathetic joy is spoken of only after compassion.

Question: why is it that, discussed in terms of dhyāna, delight is the coarser of the two, while, discussed in terms of the immeasurable minds, delight is instead the finer? Answer: within dhyāna, concentration itself is what is most prized — a tranquil, still mind of happiness supports concentration, and so is considered superior there. Within the immeasurable minds, however, the mind takes sentient beings as its object, and delight arising through the cause and condition of sentient beings is considered superior there instead — hence it is the finer of the two in this context. Furthermore: the practitioner's concentration, still shallow at the outset, can only take sentient beings as its object through happiness. Why is this? Because, were one to take up the mark of delight too soon, the mind would scatter and become difficult to gather in; only later, as samādhi as its object gradually deepens, can delight leap up without the mind becoming scattered or disordered — hence it is considered the finer of the two here.

The happiness/delight distinction, worked out here through no fewer than six overlapping criteria (body versus mind, sense-consciousness versus mind-consciousness, coarse versus fine, cause versus result, and so on), is the same pair (樂/喜) already distinguished for the first dhyāna's own factors in fascicle 5 — the hungry-person simile there (joy at first securing food, happiness in actually savoring it) maps directly onto this section's cause/result distinction. The reversal of which one counts as "coarse" depending on context (delight is coarse relative to dhyāna's own priorities, but fine relative to the immeasurable minds' priorities) is a genuinely careful point: "coarse" and "fine" are not fixed properties of a mental state but relative to what a given practice is actually trying to optimize for.

quiz.q: From where does the mind corresponding with compassion arise?
options: from sympathetic joy, seeing beings delighted
arising from the concentration of loving-kindness, one still sees beings suffering in body and mind, and pity arises
from equanimity, seeing beings neither suffering nor happy
from the concentration of no-thought
quiz.why: Within loving-kindness one wishes beings happy; arising from it one still sees them suffering in body and mind, and pity arises.

quiz.q: When the practitioner reflects, "I have been without eyes," what does this refer to?
options: not yet having the heavenly eye
an eye ailment
beings of all kinds suffer, yet I neither knew nor saw it and never resolved to rescue them
not seeing buddha-nature
quiz.why: It is self-reproach: beings everywhere suffer, yet I neither knew nor saw it and spent the long night idle, never resolving to rescue them.

quiz.q: In cultivating compassion, how should one regard those experiencing happiness or neither, for it to count as cultivating well?
options: pity only those who suffer
rejoice for the happy
recognize all three kinds as suffering and pity them without distinction
ignore the neutral
quiz.why: Pitying only the suffering is not cultivating well; seeing all three kinds as suffering and pitying them equally is.

quiz.q: An objector says seeing all beings happy is inverted, since their lots differ. What simile does the text use?
options: friction-fire: kindled with soft grass and dried dung, it grows until it burns even damp wood
a bird on a rope
treasure in a sack
silk gauze and plantain
quiz.why: It is the path of genuine understanding, not inversion: like friction-fire that starts on soft grass and grows until it burns damp wood, loving-kindness first reaches loved ones and widens to all.

quiz.q: After entering the concentration of compassion, what contemplation gives rise to sympathetic joy?
options: beings feel neither suffering nor happiness
one is already liberated
beings' suffering is permanent
though beings suffer, this suffering is illusory, originally absent and only now present, and easily removed
quiz.why: One deeply contemplates that suffering is illusory, originally absent and only now present, and so easily removed, which allows beings to pass into happiness and delight.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT among the similes showing that suffering has no fixed nature?
options: a poor person given treasure and taught generosity
a sick person cured by the right medicine
a bird in a cage escaping when it breaks
one burning with fever given cool water
quiz.why: §7 gives medicine for illness, cool water for fever, treasure for poverty, and the pure Dharma for delusion. The bird and cage appear in §9 and §13.

quiz.q: According to the Mahāyāna treatise, what is the basic difference between happiness and delight?
options: no difference
bodily happiness is happiness, mental happiness delight; with the five consciousnesses happiness, with mind-consciousness delight
form realm versus formless realm
opposites of suffering and sorrow
quiz.why: Bodily happiness is "happiness," mental happiness "delight"; with the five consciousnesses it is happiness, with mind-consciousness delight; further distinctions follow.

quiz.q: Why does sympathetic joy follow compassion rather than loving-kindness directly? What simile is used?
options: a mother wishing her child well is not yet delight; after grieving over its illness, its recovery brings great delight
a loving father seeking no reward
a wish-fulfilling jewel for the poor
friction-fire
quiz.why: Happiness comes first and delight later, with compassion between them, like a mother whose delight comes only after her sick child recovers. The loving father appears in the equanimity section.

quiz.q: Why is delight the coarser in dhyāna but the finer in the immeasurable minds?
options: there is no delight in dhyāna
dhyāna prizes concentration, which tranquil happiness supports; the immeasurable minds take beings as object, so delight arising for beings is superior
the immeasurable minds need no concentration
they are one dharma
quiz.why: In dhyāna concentration is prized and tranquil happiness supports it; in the immeasurable minds the mind takes beings as object, so delight arising for them is superior.
